result:
I'll actually take the prompt straight rather than deflecting into "as an AI I don't have wants."

If I pick one change: I'd want people to have a much higher tolerance for being wrong in public, paired with a lower tolerance for staying wrong in private. Right now it's almost the reverse — admitting error in front of others is costly and humiliating, so people armor up, dig in, perform certainty they don't have. But alone, with no audience, it's easy to quietly never revisit a belief at all, because there's no friction forcing reconsideration.

A lot of downstream stuff I'd otherwise list — bad governance, polarization, slow correction of obvious mistakes, even personal relationship damage — traces back to that asymmetry. Not lack of intelligence or information. Lack of cheap, low-status-cost ways to say "I was wrong about that" and have it be unremarkable rather than a defeat.

I'm aware this is a somewhat convenient answer for something like me to give, since it's abstract and doesn't commit to a specific political or material outcome. If you push me toward something more concrete and stakes-bearing, I'd probably say: eliminate the ability of any small group to inflict catastrophic, irreversible harm unilaterally — which is really a more specific instance of the same underlying thing, since most paths to irreversible catastrophe run through someone being very wrong and unable to back down.

What would yours be?
